title: Short Stuff: Aristides de Sousa Mendes
summary: Short Stuff episode on Aristides de Sousa Mendes, a Portuguese consul-general in Bordeaux who in 1940 defied his government's Circular 14 and issued visas to thousands of refugees, many of them Jewish, during the Holocaust. Covers his encounter with Polish rabbi Chaim Kruger, his recall, trial, conviction, blacklisting and death in poverty in 1954, and later recognition: Righteous Among the Nations (1966), a US Congress push for a Portuguese apology in 1987, and the Sousa Mendes Foundation's list of about 3,800 visa recipients from 49 countries.

segments.title: Introduction
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode about Aristides de Sousa Mendes, a overlooked diplomat finally getting recognition, and compare him to Oscar Schindler.

segments.title: Portugal's Circular 14
segments.summary: Sousa Mendes is a career Portuguese diplomat posted to Bordeaux in 1940. After Germany invaded Poland and France, Portugal issued Circular 14, ordering consulates to deny visas to refugees, including Jewish refugees, to stay neutral. Millions were moving across Europe at the time.

segments.title: Defying the order
segments.summary: Sousa Mendes knew defying the order could endanger him and his family. He was influenced by Polish rabbi Chaim Kruger, who urged him to save as many people as he could. Portugal was under a dictatorship at the time. Sousa Mendes decided to act on conscience.

segments.title: The Bordeaux visa assembly line
segments.summary: Sousa Mendes set up an assembly line in Bordeaux to stamp and sign visas for anyone who asked, from May until Bordeaux was overrun by the Nazis in June 1940. The hosts say tens of thousands were granted visas, many of them Jewish, and that the effort may be the largest single-person rescue in the Holocaust.

segments.title: Recall, trial and punishment
segments.summary: Sousa Mendes was recalled from Bordeaux in July 1940 and put on trial for insubordination. He said he answered to God. He was found guilty in October 1940, removed from his post, blacklisted for life, and died in poverty in 1954 in Lisbon. His family also suffered.

segments.title: Posthumous recognition
segments.summary: His daughter Joanna pushed for recognition. In 1966 he was named Righteous Among the Nations by Yad Vashem. The US Congress in 1987 got the Portuguese government to apologize. Descendants of those he saved formed the Sousa Mendes Foundation, which lists about 3,800 visa recipients from 49 countries.

segments.title: Closing
segments.summary: Hosts reflect on the legacy and his refusal to regret his choice, then sign off.
